title: I finally don’t care about them
author: BSwayzeYo
selftext: Hey y’all. I don’t know if you’ve noticed yet, but they (the haters), really don’t matter much anymore. Their numbers are shrinking, they are having to scream louder and louder, the content creators can’t avoid including games made with ai without risking their livelihoods, and it sure seems to me like at least 50% of today’s hate comments are just fake news from bot farms trying to drive engagement. It’s almost over. They’re almost done. Plough on my friends. 🏌️🎣😎🎉

replies.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
replies.body:
People want to be able to build game and have them judged on merit, simple as that.

People want to be respected for their output, not hated on for their choice of tool.

We all know a wave of slop is coming, no defending that but there has always been slop in gaming, it just went from asset flips to low quality slapped together AI games.

replies.author: OkVariety8064
replies.body:
> People want to be able to build game and have them judged on merit, simple as that.

If anyone can build their game with just a few prompts, why would anyone want your game specifically? And even if they do, their very own improved version is just a few prompts away.

> People want to be respected for their output, not hated on for their choice of tool.

If it stops being your output to the degree it is trivially easy for anyone to make something similar, why would anyone respect your for that?

> We all know a wave of slop is coming, no defending that but there has always been slop in gaming, it just went from asset flips to low quality slapped together AI games.

You hope for AI development to get to the point where literally anyone can build a game. Currently, the cost of tools (engines and so on) is pretty much zero, but there is still the limiting factor of skill. Once that is gone, what will be left?

Seriously, what will be left? Prompting isn't exactly a complex skill and AI can help with that too. If the cost (tools, skills and opportunity) gets lowered to the point where *literally anyone* can get the AI to build a game, what is left? Anything interesting will be cloned within hours. Games will be the equal of memes, something thrown together in a few hours and endlessly varied and copied.

No on will respect you, just like no one respects the original author of a meme. They will only care about posting their take on it.

Or are you perhaps hoping that AI will advance to a level *just complicated enough* for you but not everyone else to use it, and then you will find fame and fortune as the bestest AI prompter there is? Good luck with that.

replies.author: johnesco
replies.body:
Yes AI is a different tool because of what it can generate, but it generates base on what it's been trained on. Coming up with new ideas, for now, is still a very human thing and many people just trying to copy will eventually hit copyright issues.

Think about how as computer prices dropped and even stand alone word processors like the Smith Corona came to market, now everyone can write a book right? Do they? Or do they write resumes, recipes, little things meant only for them. Being able to type your own things didn't replace books. Being able to prompt out a book will also not replace books. A book is still the taste and organization of the writer. 

Anyone being "able" to is still not the same as everyone have to time, ideas and follow through to do it.

replies.author: chaicpp

I'm not saying it's easy for devs, but it's going to get MUCH more difficult getting noticed. I love these tools and everybody should have an opportunity to create, but the rat race is going to get bigger.

I guess we need a new storefront system, not sure what it is though lol

Btw, speaking of books, now publishers are telling writers to re-write certain portions of their books despite being human made, but now it needs to read less AI-ish.

replies.author: johnesco
replies.body: It's certainly not one to one. AI brings new things that never existed and AI can be seen as a "tool" but it's a tool unlike one we have ever seen.

replies.author: The_Grey_Archive
replies.body:
I have 25 years of game dev experience working in QA and leading QA for major titles. Nothing is stopping china sweatshops cloning your game and making a new one. Using AI is no different. A game dev with AI can make a compelling game with depth, and its no different than before. Anyone can make a game now, but can they make a good game, that is totally different. 

Since i assume you never worked on a game, you have no idea what actually happens. let me give you one example. An art director never draws anything themselves, they have senior and junior artists who draw for them and the director just offers critiques on the art and approves what is good. With AI i am filling that role now as art director and tell the AI what to make and how to make it in a way that i approve.

Nothing is different in this scenario, except im using AI instead of artists since im a solo dev and can get an image for 1 dollar, in 2 minutes, which would cost a lot more money and time to have a human artist do it.

replies.author: OkVariety8064
replies.body:
> I have 25 years of game dev experience working in QA and leading QA for major titles. Nothing is stopping china sweatshops cloning your game and making a new one. Using AI is no different.

Those sweatshops are needed, because cloning a game still has a cost. They are limited in what they can clone, and even so, they approach this as a business and build their projects with monetary gain in mind.

Those clones are made because games still have value. If AI develops at the rate it looks like developing, very soon no game will have value. When the cost of production drops to zero, the value of the product likewise drops to zero.

> A game dev with AI can make a compelling game with depth, and its no different than before. Anyone can make a game now, but can they make a good game, that is totally different.

And it will stop here? AI will advance this far but not further? We are already seeing projects made with just a few prompts, with AI iterating on gameplay mechanics and content.

We are also seeing all those decompiled classic games updated with AI. If AI becomes so accessible anyone can do that to any game with a few prompts and agents running for a few days, games will become like memes, or TikTok trends. Cheap momentary attention endlessly varied and remixed in a feeding frenzy that pays no attention to who came up with the original idea or game.

> An art director never draws anything themselves, they have senior and junior artists who draw for them and the director just offers critiques on the art and approves what is good. With AI i am filling that role now as art director and tell the AI what to make and how to make it in a way that i approve.

You are assuming that AI will be capable of filling every role, but not yours?

I'll give you a different example. An investor never makes a game themselves, but they might have an idea of what sort of game they would like to see. With AI I am filling that role now as investor and tell the AI what to make and how to make it in a way that i approve.

You assume the entire chain will be automated up to the point of you, the game developer, but no further. That AI will devour all those jobs and positions, but leave you with a job. That's a lot of confidence there.

> Nothing is different in this scenario, except im using AI instead of artists since im a solo dev and can get an image for 1 dollar, in 2 minutes, which would cost a lot more money and time to have a human artist do it.

And if it continues to develop like this, I can give AI a description, a couple of existing games to decompile for mechanics, my ideas for improvements, and for a few hundred dollars of processing time get a new game "I made".

Having you, the human game developer do the game, would cost a lot more money and time. Do you see where this is going?

replies.author: The_Grey_Archive
replies.body:
Yes, games wont be gated by high production costs nor high skill requirements. Thats not a bad thing.

  
Games in the US as a career is effectively over. All of the jobs and high finance willing to put money into games has left the states and moved to Europe. There are no more game dev jobs here right now. So your doom and gloom about games is already here. Allowing people to make games for far less money, overhead and personnel is not a bad thing. 

Your other argument is that the games space will be flooded by people who dont play games and those will be successful and push out people who know how to make games. This is again just not true. Good games take off because they are good, not because some asset flip slop chinese game company makes a clone for 10% of the cost.

Since all the jobs are now overseas, why would i care if I can make a game myself, that would have taken a whole group of people and a whole lot of more money for. You're trying to argue with me as the game dev, but missing out on me the person without a job in the games industry for years and having no faith that games will come back around in my lifetime. I am old, ancient in game standards. If games ever comes back as a career in the US i will be too old to take part. Being old, there are also health issues to take into account, which i have many.

So instead of just bitching about AI, i am using AI to make a game I have wanted for 20 years and leave something for my wife and step-son after i am gone. And your argument is, THIS IS GONNA FLOOD THE MARKET BRA. laughable.

replies.author: OkVariety8064
replies.body:
You can look at it either way. I don't really believe it will go that far, AI is very helpful in programming, but it doesn't program for you to the degree you could truly just ask it for a thing, at least in my (non-gamedev) work. Likewise in gamedev, the current AI use is a tool, even if it automates a lot. I see your point from the perspective of enjoying the opportunity and making exactly the game you want, free from the constraints of big teams or budgets.

But then there is the other side of the coin, this feeling that AI devalues everything it touches. That all will be buried under an avalanche of slop. Or worse yet, the most apocalyptic scenario of all, that the slop stops being slop and gets so good it can genuinely replace human effort. That is still scifi at the moment. But then again, we got to this point in just a few years, so where will it go from here?

You are correct, I don't work in the games industry. I have been involved in a minor way a long time ago, but never considered games seriously as a career. Too uncertain even years back. Now, with the advances in AI, I've been looking at it again in the sense that it might be fun to try some small projects, and actually get something done relatively quickly.

But then I vacillate between that and the sense that I might just be joining the last hurrah of human creativity before it's all over. That AI can automate all this, but not me? If it went this far, maybe it will automate what little I could contribute, too. And then there is of course the whole "social mediaification" of gaming, Steam already feels like a YouTube style content farm. Developers chase the platform metrics, wishlists and reviews (likes and subscriptions), a few outsized successes find an audience, and the only one who benefits consistently is the platform.

Sorry to hear the gamedev jobs market is that bad in the US. I don't think it's great in Europe either, but not entirely collapsed. Maybe games are turning more into what music or social media are, a hobby you do outside your real work, and something only a few semi-random successes can live on. If so, looks like AI might be accelerating that change more than causing it.

replies.author: Chemical-Reindeer-56
replies.body:
I want to step in this conversation for my perspective of social studies. Do you know what happened when we reach a state that Karl Marx defined as “having more than enough”, which is called >!superabundance!< >!in his The Communist Manifesto? Answer is the transformation from socialism to communism:”From!< each according to his ability, to each according to his needs.” Why would humans work 8 hrs a day to have what they want while they can just let an AI work that job for 15 mins (I’m being pessimistic here, when AI is that powerful to create communism, it won’t even take 15 mins, lol)? 

Of course, you might have several things or arguments to say about this idea but the general idea is the society will take a new FORM: either a transformation into communism or doom of humanity by corruption of centralised power of AI companies, or the slavery of humanity by borns of AGIs.

I study Philosophy, thought a lot about that though, valid concern.

replies.author: OkVariety8064
replies.body:
That is an interesting question, but at present it is still pretty much science fiction. Any society like that requires AGI, which remains a fantasy at present, and I don't at least personally find it very likely we'll get there any time soon. Of course this has been the subject of many scifi stories, Terminator is the pessimistic take, Star Trek and especially Iain Banks's Culture more positive ones.

The fact that current LLMs can do several useful tasks, assist in programming and so on, is still far, far away from replacing human work. The vast majority of work is not automatable with the sort of AI we now have. Doctor, teacher, plumber, carpenter, farmer, soldier, and so on and on are nowhere near to be replaced. The translator might see a dramatic shift in his work, and bus drivers and the like might be out of a job if self-driving ever gets to work at that level, but these are specific jobs. AI like this will no more lead to fully automated luxury communism than cars replacing horses did.

Of course, no one can tell how far AI will now go. While I don't find it likely, clearly these LLMs are on some level simulating human thought. If one of those long-shot projects like recursive self-improvement does work, then all bets are off. I still fear that any sort of smarter than human AGI would destroy humanity psychologically by its mere existence: If there is a new lifeform that is better, faster, more intelligent, more capable than you in anything you could ever hope to achieve, what purpose is there for a human to strive for anything?

replies.author: Idiberug

>Once that is gone, what will be left? Seriously, what will be left?

Nothing. AI makes everything it touches trivial.

Perhaps the widespread interest in game development and video games in general is just a sign of the infantilisation of our society, and making games so easy to make that nobody above the age of 10 cares anymore will be for the better.

replies.author: Bruoche
replies.body:
I think there's nuance to be had between expecting creators to design their games and creator manufacturing their games. 

If you're doing the design in great detail and AI just translate your specs into code without any interpretation it's one thing, using AI to one shot prompt a vague game concept is very different then just using a factory to industrialise the distribution of your game. 

Factories are made to make sure things are made faster, but also more reliably. They allow making sure every board game sold would hopefully have the same quality in line with the designer's intent.

AI on the other hand doesn't make sure to manufacture intent, it produces likely satisfactory results based on a prompt. On it's face that's similar but if you're not being very specific most of the game made will just be AI's 'best guess'

replies.author: bubuplush
replies.body:
I'm not even heavily against AI (except when they just wrote a prompt or 'stole' insanely good art and 'slop' it into something ugly only to sell it) but it feels ridiculous at this point. Yesterday I wrote 3 sentences into Claude, told it to make a pixel art side scroller where you play a mage with 4 spells. "give it cool fancy pixel explosion effects" lmao. It pumped out an insanely good game with music, good basic UI design and nice-looking character sprites.

Idk I know that it'll be a normal thing in the future, but I felt a bit.. dirty and cheap doing this? Like there was pretty much no creative process involved. I feel like a kid that taps the paper with a pencil and a Mona Lisa appears within the blink of an eye. Maybe the Mona Lisa has a weird-looking eye, but almost no one would notice. ... Yay..? Like right now I can just type the most basic prompts ever, or even ask an AI to come up with unique ideas, and flood the market with 20 simple, yet visually bombastic (for average users) phone games.

replies.body:
This was a problem for a few years before the AI boom with the "asset flippers."

Honestly most AI games are much better than the old asset flippers.

comments.author: CandidateDue2480
comments.body:
You do your thang, everyone should try to make greatness out of every tool that comes into existence. 

I'm a game dev with 10+ years and many shipped games, I'm using AI for many things that replace how I used to work. I'll tell you that on the other side of having the skills to build its quite depressing as a workflow. I can see how exciting it is to open doors for people who didn't have the skills - moreso than any of the last generations of tool developments.

But I will be curious how people feel after their initial excitement at being able to make a thing fades, and they put in the many hard years of iteration required to make a game that is both critically well-received, and sells well. So far AI isn't finishing games to the level of hitting good, shippable, widely adopted status. Because the last 20% of finishing a game is harder than the first 80% combined, and it's not even close.

There's certainly AI adoption in parts of core games development, and that will grow on the art side over time. The tech side is rife with it.

As it stands, that no AI game has come to market that is a critical success. I'm sure there's some commercial success by now, but nothing newsworthy as we'd see it everywhere from huge AI proponents.

Ultimately making a great game is still as hard as its ever been. I hope people enjoy doing what they're doing, and we'll see what happens as people start hitting the harder parts of production.

  
Good luck!

replies.author: Illustrious_Rain6329
replies.body:
As a software engineer with 20+ years building apps, it's worth noting that the situation isn't too much different with non-game software. The hardest part of building any decent sellable software, games or not, is always the last 10% -- and actually selling it is a whole nother problem.

AI is great at the first 80% and getting better at the next 10%, but it will be a long time before it can conquer the last 10% because that takes a unique kind of patient and intentional judgement, iteration, and persistence that machines simply don't have the *will* (literally) to manage. Yet.

And honestly, I'm kinda okay with that. The early piece is providing the vision, the last piece is providing the gumption, and I think it's probably fine if those two remain in human bands for the foreseeable.

replies.author: CandidateDue2480
replies.body:
Yep, the difficulty part of the software development for sure, it's similar, I've also worked in software.

It's not going to change the end of the line much because a game has a very different requirement to software, making it a very different development process entirely.

Games have to be "fun". And there's a whole lot more software out there that we use than there are the ratio of \[Games that have attempted to be made\]: \[Games that have completed, succeeded, and are fun\]

replies.body:
One thing I'm fairly excited about is that some wannabe game developers with an idea, which must be very many—who didn't have the skills or time to go through a CS, physics, math, philosophy, art, or writing degree—will be able to make their ideas a reality on their own. And maybe eventually with a team, sell a fun game that many will enjoy.  
This kid could make his dreams a reality: https://youtu.be/lGar7KC6Wiw  
  
Even if you can't make a living at it (some individual devs are very lucky like who made Thrill of the Fight VR, Flappy Bird, Wordle), realizing your dreams in whole or part is really fulfilling.

replies.author: CandidateDue2480
replies.body:
This ability to create stuff quickly and easily has existed for many years. Yes, its easier than ever to hack a prototype with AI.

 But the tools were already so easy to use that they're basically a barrier threshold of the bare minimum effort you'll need to take a game beyond shitty prototype into something that'll sell. Roblox and Fortnite UGC are kid's play compared to normal dev, but still require some effort to get it to be decent quality.

I expect the lower barrier to entry isn't going to increase the general laziness or unwillingness of someone to push past the exciting first phase of hacking a prototype and actually doing all the unsexy work to finish.

This is just my opinion, people think the opposite is true, time will tell but so far imo the tooling has been present long enough that we should already be seeing the shifts that the most fanatic of folks think will happen.

replies.author: EdOfO
replies.body: Perhaps. But maybe that tedious stage isn't necessary for people to feel fulfilled bringing their idea to reality.

replies.author: CandidateDue2480
replies.body:
Agreed! People get to make stuff for the joy of it.

It's the same as anything else. A lot of people start a thing for the wrong reasons - make money, be famous, prove they have the best ideas, etc. Most successful Twitch streamers will tell you they just enjoyed doing it.

But enjoying doing the thing gets you past the rough parts that turn it into the other goals.

I would conjecture a lot of people want to monetize their game dev, many just want to do it as a hobby. The problem is people conflate the two things very quickly when talking about all this.

replies.author: Nightstar31415
replies.body:
Well said :) I am one of those who started to create thanks to ai. I have creativity and ideas for design, but not the "boring" parts. But as you said, making it good and unique is the hard part. Having a game loop that is fun, smooth gameplay and progression that makes sense. That takes a lot of time and experimentation.

AI allowed me to get the skeleton for my idea alive, but I will probably spend years perfecting it.

replies.author: CandidateDue2480
replies.body:
Mastering the boring parts is what makes truly great design. Look up "The Door Problem" by Liz England.

All of those details for every feature is like the Ship of Thesseus.

How many of the "boring" things do you pass over to an AI until it becomes just another slop? There's no easy answer to that, but players will tell.

Ideas are the easiest part of games.

replies.author: EdOfO
replies.body:
Marketing. Whether you make it from scratch or with AI, you need a lot of marketing. Lots of studios have lost a lot more than a vibecoder will on their game release.  
  
It could be the coolest new game idea with unique mechanics and great story and characters and everything, but if it's not on anyone's wishlist, if no one is talking about it before it is released, it's no going to sell.  
  
You can't vibe-market. You can OpenClaw spam and see how poorly that goes. In the age of AI, soft skills are king.

replies.author: CandidateDue2480
replies.body: Yep.

replies.author: EdOfO
replies.body: Since you've only been in gamedev for the last 10 years, have you talked to any old hands who developed using the Waterfall model instead of Agile? I knew some devs back in the day and the last 2-3 months before their release date was insane. Almost no sleep and only sleeping in their offices. Hard on family life. I wonder if Agile development is easier on the work-life balance since you keep developing after release and players are more forgiving of bugs expecting them to be fixed eventually.

replies.author: CandidateDue2480
replies.body:
Both are a mess in the right situation and any experienced dev will tell you: "it depends."

In my 10 years ive founded a studio thats now 200 staff, was lead producer, and have directed other projects. So my 10 years is quite a bit of mileage. And I've only ever heard inexperienced devs yap about one production methodology vs another, and all veterans just say "basically anything works and everything can fall apart."

No paper process is magically solving problems for you when the deadline comes. And "it depends" depends on what exactly the shape of your game coming to close, what details need to change, culture of team, etc.

Closing a game is rarely not a solid crunch. Its just a matter of how long, how hard,  how many teams impacted.

Ive seen agile and waterfall succeed or fail, directly and indirectly. Most what I've seen fail are producer types who focus too much on methodology instead of building what the team needs at a given time.
